root.text:
You're standing in my doorway with your weight on the back foot and your eyes doing the room. That's a guard. That's a man expecting to be hit by architecture.

Sit down, Onions. Nothing in here has ever hit anybody who was sitting.

options.text: "Your corridor doesn't turn and brings me back facing forward."
"The wall behind the far booth goes transparent."
"Your security has a laminated card about denying things that happened."
Leave the conversation at the exact moment it stops being useful.

check.success_text:
You are standing and moving before the sentence she is building has finished being built, and you are through the door on the beat where the music changes, which is the only beat on which anybody leaves this room unremarked.

From the corridor, briefly, you hear her say — to nobody, in a completely different voice — "Well. *He* knows how to leave."
check.failure_text: You go to leave and the room does what the room does: the music holds, the conversation has one more turn in it, and you take the turn, and by the time you are out you have been seen leaving by everybody who was going to see it.

clue.title: A completely different voice
clue.text: Leaving the Möbius unremarked, you hear Ginny speak to an empty room in a voice that is not the one she uses on people.

options.text: "You run this floor. You don't run what I'm doing on it."

check.success_text:
She looks at you for slightly longer than the sentence deserved.

"Good," she says. "Say it like that to the gators and they'll write it down and file it and forget it, which is what you want. Say it like that to me and I'll respect it, which is worse for you, because now I'm interested."

She puts the gin down.

"Weight was right. Chin was wrong — you lifted it, which is a tell, and it says the standing's borrowed. Doesn't matter in here. Will matter in about four days when somebody asks you who you are and you have to answer without a wobble in it. Practise on me. I'm cheap."
check.failure_text:
"Mm," says Ginny, and does not look up from the till. "You said that with your weight on the back foot."

And that is the whole of the exchange, and the room absorbs it without a ripple, and somewhere behind you a man in a suit that fits too well makes a note of nothing at all.

clue.title: The standing is borrowed
clue.text: Ginny reads Oliver's authority as borrowed — the weight right, the chin lifted, a tell. She expects it to be tested within four days by somebody asking who he is.

options.text: Leave before the room decides something.

corridor.text:
Correct. It doesn't turn and it brings you back forward. That's the building. That's what the building is *called*, it's on the sign in red, we did not hide it.

And here's the thing you're about to do, and I'd rather you didn't, so I'm going to name it first: you're about to treat that as a problem. It isn't. A problem is something you can be hit by. That corridor has never hit anybody. Whereas my ice machine is a problem, and my licensing is a problem, and the fact that a man came in here Tuesday and *walked at a wall* is very much a problem, and none of those are impossible and all of them are mine.

passive.text: She is not incurious. She is triaging. This is a woman who worked out years ago exactly how much of this she can afford to look at, and has held the line every day since, and is holding it now, in front of you, at some cost.

options.text: "You know exactly what this building is."

check.success_text:
"'Course I know."

She puts the gin down. Not hard — placed, the way you place a thing you might need both hands away from.

"I've managed this floor eleven years. You think I haven't paced the corridor? I've paced it with a tape. I've paced it with two men and a tape. I know precisely what my building is, Onions, and here's what I do about it: I open at six, I run the bar, I pay eleven people, and I do not look at the back wall.

That's not denial. Denial's Bud Onkuhdonk, up at the Inn, arguing with weather. This is a *stance*. I know what's coming through that wall and I have decided where my feet go, and my feet go here, in front of the till, between it and them."
check.failure_text: "I know what it's called, I know what it costs to heat, and I know what time the fire inspection is." She picks the gin back up. "You came in here to be told something. Everybody does. The dancers are through there."

clue.title: A stance, not denial
clue.text: Ginny has paced the corridor with a tape and two men. She knows exactly what the club is, and has chosen to stand between it and her eleven staff rather than look at it.

options.text: "Show me the ice machine. You said it was a problem."

check.success_text:
It is a good machine badly used and it takes about four minutes to find out why: the thermostat is fine, the compressor is fine, and the drain runs uphill for eleven inches before it remembers itself.

You say so. Ginny looks at the eleven inches for a while.

"That pipe was straight in March," she says. "I had it in. I watched him fit it. It ran downhill because pipes do."

She crouches, follows it with two fingers, and stops where it lifts.

"Right. So my building's been quietly redecorating the plumbing and the only reason anybody knows is that ice is the one thing in here that won't lie about which way is down."
check.failure_text: You get the panel off and a great deal of cold air and a diagnosis of 'it's the drain, probably', which Ginny receives with the exact courtesy of a woman who has had that diagnosis from three engineers and a cousin.

clue.title: Ice will not lie about which way is down
clue.text: The Möbius ice machine fails because its drain now runs uphill for eleven inches. The pipe was fitted straight in March. Ice is the only thing in the building that cannot be persuaded about the direction of down.

corridor_stance.text:
Now. Since we're being adults about it, one piece of advice, free, and you'll ignore it because men who investigate always do.

Everything in this town that's gone wrong for somebody has gone wrong at the moment they *lunged*. Not when they looked — looking's free, look all you like, I look. When they lunged. Reached, grabbed, ran at, shouted at.

You fight a thing bigger than you by making it come to you. It's not brave and it's not satisfying and it is the only thing that has ever worked. Keep your weight down, Onions.

wall.text:
Yes.

That's it. That's the whole answer. Yes, it does that, roughly nine times a night, roughly two seconds a go, and I could set a clock by it except that in this establishment that sentence has a second meaning I'd rather not have opened.

check.success_text:
"That's the question," she says, and looks at you properly for the first time. "Nobody asks that one. They all ask what's behind it. You asked how long.

Two seconds because two seconds is what a person *glances* at. Long enough that you saw it, short enough that you can't check it. That's not a physical property, Onions. Nothing physical has a duration tuned to human attention.

Somebody set it. And a thing that's been set can be set differently, and the week before you came out of that harbour it was running at four."
check.failure_text: "Because that's how long it does it for." She drinks. "You're asking a plumbing question about a wall. I've got no plumber for the wall. I've asked."

clue.title: Tuned to a glance
clue.text: The transparency lasts exactly two seconds — long enough to see, too short to verify. Nothing physical has a duration tuned to human attention. The week before Oliver surfaced, it was running at four.

options.text: Two seconds is not a glance. Two seconds is a *look*, and something is doing the looking.

check.success_text:
Turn it round. Everybody in this club has spent eleven years asking what is behind the wall, which assumes the wall is a window and you are on the outside of it.

You are not on the outside of it.

Two seconds, nine times a night, at a duration tuned exactly to human attention — that is not a leak and it is not a fault. That is a schedule. Something opens a wall onto this room on a rhythm, for precisely as long as it takes to see and not long enough to be checked, and it has been doing it since before you came out of the water.

The correct question was never what is behind it. The correct question is what it has been *looking at*, ninety times a night, for eleven years.
check.failure_text: It goes transparent, and there is black stone behind it, and it goes back, and the whole business takes about two seconds and refuses to be more sinister than that no matter how long you stand in front of it with your coat on.

clue.title: The wall is not a window you are outside of
clue.text: The Möbius wall's two-second transparency is a schedule, not a fault — tuned to be seen and not verified, nine times a night for eleven years. The question is not what is behind it but what it has been looking at.

wall_tuned.text:
Four seconds, the week before. I know because a girl on the early shift complained about it and I wrote it in the book, and I wrote 'four' because I counted, twice, on two separate nights.

Then you came up out of the water and it went to two, and it has been two every night since, and I would very much like you to tell me that's a coincidence in a way I can believe.

clue.title: It shortened when you surfaced
clue.text: The wall's transparency ran at four seconds until the day Oliver came out of the harbour. It has been two every night since.

whats_behind.text:
Vault doors, mostly. Black stone. That's the mortuary up the hill, which is a hell of a thing to have showing through your back wall at a stag party, and I have stopped apologising for it because apologising made it a topic.

And once a month, give or take — a room. Low ceiling. Green lamp. Desk.

lucid.2: She describes it without hesitating over any detail, which is how you describe a room you have looked at more than once.

check.success_text:
"Desk made out of a door on two trestles. Left trestle's split. Paper everywhere — not stacked, *drifted*, like nobody's tidied since there was a reason to. Green shade on the lamp. Cup with a ring under it. Chair pushed back.

And a typewriter."

She is watching your face while she says it, which is a fighter's habit, and she does not stop.

"That's your desk, isn't it. I've been looking at your desk through my back wall once a month for eleven years and I only worked that out about four seconds ago, from your face, and I would like it very much on the record that I did not enjoy it."
check.failure_text: "A room. Lamp, desk, paper. I've got a bar to run, Onions, I don't take inventory of the impossible, I take inventory of the gin." But her eyes went to the back wall while she said it, and came back, and she noticed you notice.

clue.title: She has been watching your desk for eleven years
clue.text: Ginny describes the room behind the wall in exact detail — including the split left trestle leg. It is Oliver's desk. She has seen it monthly for eleven years.

room_is_yours.text:
Right. Right.

OK. Guard up, weight down, and let's do this properly, because I've had eleven years of the slow version and you've had a week and I'd rather we arrived together.

If that's your desk, and it's through my wall, then either you're in two places or my wall is. And I've measured my wall.

options.text: "Revilo's Trap Built. Through the monocle. Every time."

revilo_reveal.text:
She does not ask what a monocle has to do with it. She does not ask who Revilo is. Both of those omissions are answers.

"Onions. I'm going to tell you a thing and then I'm going to ask you to leave, and the leaving isn't hostile, it's *tactical*, and I need you to take it in that spirit.

I don't own this club. I've never owned this club. I manage it, I sign for it, my name's on the licence and I've never once met the freeholder — the paperwork comes through the Coalition and the instructions come on cards with four lobes on them, and the instructions are always about the same thing.

They're always about a man. Height, coat, a cane with an onion on it. Eleven years of cards telling me what to do if a specific man ever walks in the front."

clue.title: Eleven years of instructions about you
clue.text: Ginny does not own the club. Instructions arrive on four-lobed cards, and for eleven years they have described a tall man in a coat with an onion-handled cane, and what to do if he walks in the front.

options.text: "And what do the cards say to do?"

what_do.text:
"Let him in. Let him look. Do not stop him. Do not help him."

She picks the gin back up and does not drink it.

"Eleven years, Onions. Same three lines, every card. Somebody has been holding a door open for you for eleven years and paying eleven staff to stand near it and not touch you.

Now get out of my club. Come back tomorrow — come back every day, I'm not barring you, I'm *timing* you. But the gators have had a card this week they haven't shown me, and a card they haven't shown me is the first one in eleven years, and I would like you on the other side of my door while I find out what's on it."

clue.title: A card she has not been shown
clue.text: For eleven years the cards said: let him in, let him look, do not stop him, do not help him. This week the Insta-gators received one Ginny has not been shown.

gators.text:
The laminated card. Yes. I wrote lines one through four.

I did not write line five. Line five arrived. And line five used to be one sentence and now it's two, and the second sentence is 'log the anomaly', and I have never seen the log, and I have asked four times, and each time I've been told — courteously, in that voice they do — that they'll circle back.

Eleven years of circling back, Onions. They have circled back precisely never, and they say it every single time like it's the first.

clue.title: There is a log she has never seen
clue.text: Ginny wrote the first four lines of Insta-gator doctrine. Line five arrived from elsewhere and instructs them to log anomalies that did not occur. She has asked to see the log four times and been told they will circle back.

standing.text:
"Right. Lesson's over, I've got a floor.

One thing though, and take it or don't. Whatever you're walking toward — and you are, you've got the walk — it's going to end in a room with one other person in it. They always do. And in a room with one other person, authority isn't the loud thing. It's whoever's still there at the end of the sentence.

Be there at the end of the sentence, Onions."

two_seconds_threat.text:
She does not say anything for a while, which for Ginny is a substantial expenditure.

"Eleven years," she says. "Eleven years I've had that wall and I've asked what's behind it maybe four thousand times and I have never once asked it the other way round.

Right. Well. That's my night ruined and probably my decade."

She picks the gin up and this time she drinks it.

"Guard up, Onions. And do me a favour — when you work out what it's been looking at, don't tell me in here. There's ninety people on this floor."

ice_machine.text:
"Don't say it. I know what you're going to say and I've got ninety people on that floor and a fire inspection Thursday."

She stands up, wipes her hands, and puts them flat on the top of the machine for a second, which is a thing Ben does, and which she has certainly never seen Ben do.

"Eleven inches. In my ice. Right — go on, get out, I've got a pipe to be furious at. And Onions: thanks. That's not sarcasm, I'm aware it reads as sarcasm. Nobody's fixed anything in here in eleven years."
